thread.title: The 'Secret' to a Stock Market Fortune

title: The 'Secret' to a Stock Market Fortune
text:
The 'Secret' to a Stock Market Fortune By msft The most consistently profitable activity in the stock market isn't trading, investing or actually owning stocks. The easy road to success is selling the 'secret' to success.
If you have been active in the market for a while you have probably seen a steady stream of advertising telling you about a quick and easy way to make big profits. Sometimes it's a special trading strategy, and other times it's a hot pick. All you need to do is sign up for the service to learn "the secret," and the riches are yours.
It should become evident very quickly that there is no simple secret to trading. There is no omniscient guru who will convey to you the one stock that will make you rich beyond your wildest dreams.
The secret to successful trading is that there is no simple secret. Success is a product of hard work and perseverance, and even if you are one of the best, you will still have great challenges and lose money at times. You need to work at betting the market and there are no shortcuts. There are people like TheStreet's Jim Cramer that can help you in the endeavor, but you still have to put your nose to the grindstone and make a real effort to do the necessary work. The Passive Approach
There has always been a faction of market participants that have embraced the idea that it isn't possible to 'beat' the market. Many of them have tried in various ways and given up in frustration. They are convinced that since the market always goes up over time they might as well just ride it and not waste time trying to beat it.
There has been tremendous growth in a passive approach to the market in recent years. The Vanguard Funds championed by Jack Bogle were the first index-based mutual funds introduced in the mid-1970s. There has been tremendous growth in index funds in the last 10 years and it was estimated last year by Morningstar that there is over $3 trillion in passive funds.
The biggest problem with the passive approach is that humans still have to deal with timing. We are not going to leave our funds in the market forever. There have been periods of a decade or more when a passive fund would have not produced a positive return. Over the very long term it is safe but as the old economic saying goes, in the long run we are all dead. The Buffett Approach
Other frustrated investors have moved to a variation of the passive approach but they use individual stocks rather than indices. The idea is to find one of the very few stocks that will produce substantial outperformance over the very long term. If you had picked an Apple ( AAPL ) or Microsoft ( MSFT ) at any early point there is no question you would do extremely well.
(Apple and Microsoft are holdings in Jim Cramer's Action Alerts PLUS member club . Want to be alerted before Jim Cramer buys or sells AAPL or MSFT? Learn more now. )
The problem here is that it is tremendously difficult to find these stocks on a prospective basis. In the rearview mirror it is easy to see what would have worked, but ask someone today what will be the next Apple or Microsoft and it isn't nearly as easy. The Soros Approach
TheStreet's chartist Bruce Kamich tweeted this quote the other day from George Soros: "I'm not better than the next trader, just quicker at admitting my mistakes and moving on to the next opportunity."
In my view this is the closest we will ever get to finding 'the secret' to great market success. The key isn't a particular style or hoping that a very long-term view will benefit you. The secret is to keep on slogging away. Admit mistakes quickly and move on to the next trade. You will consistently make mistakes but by admitting them quickly you will be in a better position to reap great profits on an opportunity that works.
In order to be a successful trader, you need to do several things. First, you need to have a style or approach that makes sense to you so that you can embrace it. Second, you need to have a steady supply of good ideas so that you can apply your approach. Third, you need to have a methodology that helps you manage positions -- which is just another aspect of style.
Most importantly you need to work at it day after day. Embrace your mistakes, take your losses and then move on. Traders that build great fortunes do it by grinding out gains over a very long period. They don't put it all on Red 21 and spin the wheel in hopes of a huge payoff. Instead, they dig for new ideas day after day, and then they work hard at managing them.
There are few businesses that offer you that steady supply of opportunities that trading does. Once you recognize that and find a way to embrace it, you will likely be a trader forever.
